Proposition 39
Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State's website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter's identity is established through the registration process by using their driver's license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor's Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
Proposal
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make "best efforts" using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government-Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters' identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter's registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter's identify when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
Fiscal Effects
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote-for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.

Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID

NO on PROP. 39—Stop Trump from rigging our elections. Don’t believe the lies. Prop. 39 MAKES VOTING HARDER, MORE EXPENSIVE, AND LESS SAFE for Californians.
PROP. 39 IS FUNDED BY MAGA RIGHTWING BILLIONAIRES. Follow the money. MAGA billionaires have spent millions spreading election lies. Republican operatives have pushed this voter suppression agenda for years. They want Trump to have unlimited power so they get more tax breaks for the rich while cutting funding to healthcare and schools for the rest of us.
California election officials already verify voters. Prop. 39 just ADDS EXTRA HURDLES for citizens. THE FACTS DON’T LIE. When Texas tried this, they threw out 12 times more mail ballots than California.
Prop. 39 creates new threats of identity theft. No citizen should have to choose between their privacy and their right to vote.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office found that Prop. 39 could COST HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS EACH YEAR—read it for yourself. MAGA extremists want to use your taxpayer dollars to buy Trump an expensive gift: blocking eligible voters and giving the Big Lie a win in California. We won’t fall for it.
PROP. 39 TRIES TO DISTRACT US from how Trump and his billionaire friends have failed Americans. Hospitals are closing. Fire victims are still waiting for help. Groceries and housing costs are more expensive than ever. Now they want to use Prop. 39 to control our elections and avoid accountability.
NO KINGS. NO LIES. NO PROP. 39.

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 39
VOTE NO. Donald Trump lies about elections and uses those lies to grab power.
STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB. Trump wants revenge on California—he has delayed LA wildfire relief, undone laws to keep our air and water clean, and constantly attacked our immigrant friends and neighbors. Now he wants to undo our freedoms and democracy with Prop. 39. Trump’s cronies want to rig California elections so they can seize and keep control of Congress and the White House. Trump will do whatever it takes to tear apart our right to vote, dodge accountability, and hold onto authoritarian power.
CALIFORNIANS WON’T FALL FOR IT. We have a chance to fight back and stop Trump by voting NO on Prop. 39. Don’t let California become the next state where politicians pick which voters count.
WASTES HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS.
Trump and his accomplices want California to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to chase their election lies and conspiracy theories. Californians are struggling, and Trump wants YOU to pay for his conspiracies.
PUTS YOUR IDENTITY AT RISK. Prop. 39 will make every vote by mail voter include their personal details on their return envelope—making voters easy targets for identity theft. Voters would have to choose between voting and protecting their privacy.
BLOCKS CITIZENS FROM VOTING. Prop. 39 adds new hurdles—voters would have to include a personal ID number on their ballot envelope that has to exactly match state records. Get one digit wrong, and a valid ballot could get thrown out. If you don’t take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting—you may not get a mail ballot at all. And if the address on your ID is not up to date or your name is misspelled—your vote might be rejected.
PUSHES OUT VOTERS. “Free” state IDs aren’t free: voters still pay for transportation, time off work, and costs like childcare or getting required documents. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters of color, and the millions of women who changed their names at marriage are hit hardest. These unfair barriers help politicians choose their voters instead of the other way around.
TRUMP LIES TO GRAB POWER. DON’T LET THOSE LIES TAKE AWAY YOUR VOTE.
PROTECT YOUR VOICE. PROTECT YOUR VOTE. VOTE NO.

PROP. 39 IS BIPARTISAN—NOT ABOUT DONALD TRUMP OR GAVIN NEWSOM
Prop. 39 gives California a bipartisan solution for election security. While politicians in D.C. fight over partisan control of elections, Californians can adopt our own solution: Voter ID. Prop. 39 improves the accuracy of our voter lists and requires independent audits to strengthen election management.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Issue Brief
Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.
Table Of Contents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking
California Should Continue to Promote Voter Participation and Improve the Election Process
Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. This and other research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129241283169) suggests this may be because voters view election laws through a partisan lens and their confidence may be more heavily influenced by partisan rhetoric and whether their preferred candidate wins or loses an election. 13 (javascript:void(0)) See Lonna Rae Atkeson, Eli McKown-Dawson, and Robert M. By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: October 15, 2026 at 3:13 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
A healthy democracy depends on both public participation and public trust. Without either, the system risks disaffection and loss of legitimacy.
California has made numerous moves in recent years to boost voter participation. From making it easier than ever to vote by mail to overly-liberal ballot harvesting laws, the Golden State has worked to optimize the public participation component of its election administration.
California has also maintained rising levels of public confidence in aspects of its elections. In 2017, just 47% of likely voters and 40% of adults either had “quite a lot of” or a “great deal of” confidence in how California counts votes, according to surveys by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California. By 2024, those figures rose to 63% and 53%, respectively.
Lurking beneath (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/time-trends-all-adults-1024-corrected.pdf) those 2024 numbers were bigger concerns about election integrity than those figures suggest. The same survey found that 42% of adults and 43% of likely voters said they were “somewhat concerned” or “very concerned” that it’s “too easy for people who are not eligible to vote in California elections.”
Enter Proposition 39.
The proposal seeks to improve public confidence in elections with a simple rule: voters must present a government-issued ID when voting in person or include the last four digits of a government-issued ID that corresponds to identification used at the time of registration on the ballots they intend to mail in. For those who do not have such identification, the measure calls for free identification to be provided for voting.
It also requires election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists and “use best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations. Finally, it directs regular audits by the State Auditor to ensure compliance with these rules and offer recommendations for how to improve election integrity.
There’s nothing radical about these recommendations. Thirty six states require voters to present some form of identification when voting. Such a requirement is commonplace around the world, including in Canada and Mexico. The logic of identification requirements is quite obvious: it’s simply another check to ensure that people are who they say they are when they vote. In fact, poll workers in California already ask (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/trusted-info-voter-id-reg-requirements.pdf) first-time federal election voters who didn’t include an ID number at the time of registration for ID if they show up to the polls.
Opponents of voter identification requirements counter that requiring voters to provide identification at the polls is an unacceptable barrier to democratic participation. We disagree. If people can clear the “barrier” of presenting an ID to buy cigarettes or alcohol or use a credit card or get on an airplane, they can present ID to vote.
Opponents likewise counter that requiring voters to write the last four digits of their ID on their ballots introduces a failure point or privacy risk. We are sympathetic to privacy concerns, though such concerns would be more serious if the rule was to write the total ID number. And the failure point is real — what if voters write the wrong numbers? — but fixable. Ballots can be cured.
Research on the impact of such rules has been mixed over the years, with one review published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2019 finding (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) that “strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.” Echoing this is an analysis published (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) by the journal Research & Politics in December 2024 which found “no compelling evidence that strict voter ID laws consistently suppress or boost voter turnout. Rather, the modest and opposing impacts across contexts appear to net out to minimal aggregate effects on participation, consistent with research showing that electoral reforms often produce small equilibrium effects.”

What could be the most controversial component of the measure is its mandate that election officials use “best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations using “government data.” The measure does not define these terms, thus giving the state and election officials room to figure out how to do that in the most reasonable manner possible. While this editorial board isn’t of the view that noncitizen voting is rampant, it doesn’t seem irrational to occasionally confirm people who attest to their citizenship actually are citizens.
If passed, we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period as it’s worked out. Combining the convenience of voting with basic verification isn’t voter suppression — it’s just common-sense governance. Vote Yes on Proposition 39.

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

In summary
Republican megadonors are boosting California’s voter ID measure in the hopes its success, or failure, can reveal how similar measures can perform in more moderate states.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Want to know who’s who in Republican politics? Look no further than the megadonors bankrolling California’s voter ID initiative.
Illinois billionaire packing supply magnate Richard Uihlein, who has poured tens of millions of dollars into conservative causes, has contributed $17 million to the campaign for Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), a GOP-backed ballot measure to require voters to show a driver’s license or other government ID to vote.
Uihlein’s involvement and that of other deep-pocketed Republican donors is a signal that conservatives view Prop. 39 as a test of support for future battleground states in the broader push by President Donald Trump to tighten voter restrictions.
Uihlein is joined by Airbnb co-founder and current White House official Joe Gebbia, who on Wednesday gave $8 million to the campaign. Southern California businessman Steven Bray is another top donor, having loaned the campaign more than $3 million and given $50,000 outright. The right-wing political group Reform California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/03/california-republican-endorsements/), tech entrepreneurs Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. presidential running mate Nicole Shanahan are also major donors. Combined, they have helped the campaign rake in more than $36 million — $13 million more than their opponents a month from Election Day.
Prop. 39’s supporters argue that requiring ID at polling places will ensure California’s elections are secure, and say the mandate is no different from needing an ID to fly on a plane or buy alcohol. Proponents also point out that 36 states request or require voters to show some form of identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id).
ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026)
2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/)
Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know
California voters currently need a driver’s license and Social Security number to register to vote but not when they cast their ballots. If Prop. 39 passes, voters who mail their ballots would have to write the last four digits of their Social Security or other government-issued number on their ballots.
It’s a long-awaited moment for the state’s weak Republican Party which has fought for decades to put a voter ID measure on the ballot in deep blue California.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a Republican, created Reform California and is spearheading the initiative. The freshman San Diego lawmaker’s group funded the ballot operation that collected more than a million signatures to qualify the measure after similar proposals failed in the Democratic-controlled Legislature.
Common Cause and other voting rights groups that oppose the measure fear Prop. 39 would unnecessarily block from voting citizens who can’t find or don’t have a government-issued ID. They argue that this would disproportionately impact, and unfairly penalize, people who recently moved, changed their last name or are low income — and other groups who historically have supported Democrats.
Civil rights advocates also argue the measure is unnecessary because voter fraud is rare.
“You are more likely to be struck by lightning than you are to commit voter fraud in a U.S. election,” California League of Women Voters executive director Jenny Farrell said. “There’s no need to add on these additional burdens and security checkpoints in California.”

Despite numerous studies showing there is no widespread evidence (https://apnews.com/article/voter-fraud-election-2020-joe-biden-donald-trump-7fcb6f134e528fee8237c7601db3328f) of voter fraud in U.S. elections, Claremont McKenna College political scientist John Pitney said such claims have circulated for decades in far-right circles.
Attempts to constrict voter laws through ballot measures have increased in some states ever since the expansion of voting rights to African Americans during the Civil Rights Movement.
But fears about voter fraud accelerated during the first Trump administration when the president falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen. Shortly after, DeMaio and other GOP lawmakers introduced unsuccessful bills to tighten voter restrictions before he pivoted to orchestrating a citizen-led ballot initiative last year.
“Recently Trump has promoted the idea that large numbers of undocumented people are voting, for which there isn’t any evidence,” Pitney said.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio announces that supporters of the CA Voter ID Initiative will submit more than 1.3 million signatures to qualify the measure for the November 2026 ballot during a press conference at the west steps of the state Capitol in Sacramento on March 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Democrats bankrolling the opposition to Prop. 39 are also a who’s who of California politics.
The state Democratic Party is by far the largest contributor at nearly $5.5 million, followed by the Sonoma-area Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria with $2 million.
Longtime Democratic donors Patty Quillin, a film producer and wife of Netflix CEO Reed Hastings, and Quinn Delaney, a real estate investor and philanthropist, have each pitched in $1.5 million. Labor heavyweights such as the Service Employees International Union have contributed $1 million.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra (https://calmatters.org/tag/xavier-becerra/) and Democratic Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/robert-rivas-165041) have created a joint committee to raise money for the No campaign and U.S. Sen Alex Padilla is stumping at events.
Nearly 90% of Californians now vote by mail, according to the secretary of state’s office (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/historical-absentee). That means the vast majority of voters would be required to write their Social Security or driver’s license number on their ballot should the initiative pass.
Many people aren’t going to be comfortable with that, No on 39 campaign spokesperson Tenoch Flores said.
“This is about creating new avenues to reject valid mail ballots,” Flores said.
“Yes on 39” spokesperson Meredith Shields told CalMatters that no one from the campaign could be made available for an interview. DeMaio declined an interview with CalMatters for this story. Uihlein did not respond to phone calls and emails requesting comment.
The biggest donor
Megadonor Uihlein and his wife, founders of the Wisconsin-based packaging company Uline, have poured millions into the Restoration of America PAC, a super PAC that frequently bankrolls Republican candidates in Illinois and Wisconsin. The Uihleins have donated $35 million to the PAC (https://www.fec.gov/data/individual-contributions/?committee_id=C00571588&contributor_name=uihlein&two_year_transaction_period=2026) this year alone, and Prop. 39 is the latest target in their effort to fund agenda-setting conservative causes.
Shanahan, an attorney and the former wife of Google executive Sergey Brin, has funneled $370,000 into the Yes campaign, while the Winklevoss brothers have each contributed $250,000.
The interest from the ultra-wealthy in Prop. 39 is a sign that the GOP could be looking to replicate a similar playbook in toss-up states, Sonoma State University political science Professor David McCuan said.
Republican proponents want to see how well or poorly voter ID does in Democratic-heavy California. If it does better than expected, that might mean a similar ballot measure could be fairly popular in more moderate battleground states, such as Michigan,Wisconsin or Pennsylvania.
“There is a spillover effect if you do better than expected, even if you lose,” McCuan said.
Election security becomes about Trump
Several Republican states moved to expand voter restrictions after the 2020 election, including Wyoming, Kentucky and Oklahoma. And while voter sentiment toward Trump is at historic lows, the GOP was surprisingly successful at getting the voter ID measure on the California ballot.
The “Yes on 39” TV campaign has begun airing ads (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ts64oxA4neQ) distancing the measure’s supporters from Trump, while the No campaign released an ad airing in the Bay Area (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) featuring images of Trump and characterizations of Prop. 39 as a “power grab.”
It’ll likely still be a tough road ahead for the Yes campaign. The default position for most voters is “no” on ballot propositions, meaning supporters of the measure will have to persuade enough voters to agree with them.
An April poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2d964377) showed Californians broadly support requiring voters to present identification at the polls, but it found that support dipped below 50% when respondents were given specific details about the measure, such as that it’s meant to combat alleged voter fraud. A Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) poll in September found support for Prop. 39 has dropped to 43%.
While this could be effective at turning out liberal voters, it’s unclear how even a hot-button issue will be enough to get Republicans out in a midterm election cycle with an unpopular president.
“It’s hard to pass a red-coded measure in a blue wave election,” Pitney said.

# California elections officials rejected 122,000 ballots in 2024 election. Here’s why
SACRAMENTO, Calif.
— Elections officials around California threw out 122,480 vote-by-mail ballots cast during the November general election, or 0.9% of all mail-in ballots, according to data from the Secretary of State’s office.
The vast majority of those were tossed because they arrived late, had mismatched voter signatures or no signature at all.
Elections officials are supposed to notify a voter if their mail-in ballot has a signature issue and provide an opportunity to “cure,” or fix it.
But they’re not always successful, leaving those ballots uncounted.
An analysis of mail ballot rejections during the 2024 election by USC’s Center for Inclusive Democracy found that 59% had a nonmatching voter signature, 27% were mailed or arrived after the deadline, and 11% had no signature.
The other 3% were thrown out for other unspecified reasons.

In this world, however, the stakes seem to be considerably lower.
That’s the conclusion of a new study, one of the largest to date, from the economists Enrico Cantoni and Vincent Pons, which assessed the impact of voter ID laws between 2008 and 2016 using a nationwide voter file.
The study finds that requiring voter identification has no effect on turnout — not overall, and not on “any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.”
If that shocks you, it shouldn’t.
The evidence that voter ID laws meaningfully suppress minority votes has always been shaky; a literature review in 2017 that filtered out studies with obvious design flaws reported “modest, if any, turnout effects of voter identification laws” in the best research on the subject.
So a voter ID requirement might possibly affect the closest of close races, based on what we’ve learned up till now — but if the Cantoni and Pons results hold up, the real effect is basically nil.

# California elections officials rejected 122,000 ballots in 2024 election. Here’s why
SACRAMENTO, Calif.
— Elections officials around California threw out 122,480 vote-by-mail ballots cast during the November general election, or 0.9% of all mail-in ballots, according to data from the Secretary of State’s office.
The vast majority of those were tossed because they arrived late, had mismatched voter signatures or no signature at all.
Elections officials are supposed to notify a voter if their mail-in ballot has a signature issue and provide an opportunity to “cure,” or fix it.
But they’re not always successful, leaving those ballots uncounted.
An analysis of mail ballot rejections during the 2024 election by USC’s Center for Inclusive Democracy found that 59% had a nonmatching voter signature, 27% were mailed or arrived after the deadline, and 11% had no signature.
The other 3% were thrown out for other unspecified reasons.

In this world, however, the stakes seem to be considerably lower.
That’s the conclusion of a new study, one of the largest to date, from the economists Enrico Cantoni and Vincent Pons, which assessed the impact of voter ID laws between 2008 and 2016 using a nationwide voter file.
The study finds that requiring voter identification has no effect on turnout — not overall, and not on “any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.”
If that shocks you, it shouldn’t.
The evidence that voter ID laws meaningfully suppress minority votes has always been shaky; a literature review in 2017 that filtered out studies with obvious design flaws reported “modest, if any, turnout effects of voter identification laws” in the best research on the subject.
So a voter ID requirement might possibly affect the closest of close races, based on what we’ve learned up till now — but if the Cantoni and Pons results hold up, the real effect is basically nil.

In this world, however, the stakes seem to be considerably lower.
That’s the conclusion of a new study, one of the largest to date, from the economists Enrico Cantoni and Vincent Pons, which assessed the impact of voter ID laws between 2008 and 2016 using a nationwide voter file.
The study finds that requiring voter identification has no effect on turnout — not overall, and not on “any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.”
If that shocks you, it shouldn’t.
The evidence that voter ID laws meaningfully suppress minority votes has always been shaky; a literature review in 2017 that filtered out studies with obvious design flaws reported “modest, if any, turnout effects of voter identification laws” in the best research on the subject.
So a voter ID requirement might possibly affect the closest of close races, based on what we’ve learned up till now — but if the Cantoni and Pons results hold up, the real effect is basically nil.

# California elections officials rejected 122,000 ballots in 2024 election. Here’s why
SACRAMENTO, Calif.
— Elections officials around California threw out 122,480 vote-by-mail ballots cast during the November general election, or 0.9% of all mail-in ballots, according to data from the Secretary of State’s office.
The vast majority of those were tossed because they arrived late, had mismatched voter signatures or no signature at all.
Elections officials are supposed to notify a voter if their mail-in ballot has a signature issue and provide an opportunity to “cure,” or fix it.
But they’re not always successful, leaving those ballots uncounted.
An analysis of mail ballot rejections during the 2024 election by USC’s Center for Inclusive Democracy found that 59% had a nonmatching voter signature, 27% were mailed or arrived after the deadline, and 11% had no signature.
The other 3% were thrown out for other unspecified reasons.

In this world, however, the stakes seem to be considerably lower.
That’s the conclusion of a new study, one of the largest to date, from the economists Enrico Cantoni and Vincent Pons, which assessed the impact of voter ID laws between 2008 and 2016 using a nationwide voter file.
The study finds that requiring voter identification has no effect on turnout — not overall, and not on “any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.”
If that shocks you, it shouldn’t.
The evidence that voter ID laws meaningfully suppress minority votes has always been shaky; a literature review in 2017 that filtered out studies with obvious design flaws reported “modest, if any, turnout effects of voter identification laws” in the best research on the subject.
So a voter ID requirement might possibly affect the closest of close races, based on what we’ve learned up till now — but if the Cantoni and Pons results hold up, the real effect is basically nil.

Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) will help alleviate doubts in California’s vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/). Guest Commentary written by Bill Jones Bill Jones is a former California secretary of state. During two terms as California’s chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other. A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That’s why I’m supporting Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) on this November’s ballot. I hope Californians will join me. Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce. It doesn’t disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID (http://ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id) and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place. This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.
