Below, a civic engagement advocate worries Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system. The opposing view: A former state elections chief says the measure will help alleviate doubts in California’s vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/). Guest Commentary written by Marisol Ramirez Marisol Ramirez is a member of the Inland Empire Latino Giving Circle, advancing democratic participation, community leadership and equitable access to civic institutions. This November, Californians will head to the ballot box and participate in another election with real consequences for our communities. As a Latina and local philanthropist in the Inland Empire who has spent nearly two decades working to strengthen civic participation, I have learned that democracy is strongest when elections are both accessible and secure. From celebrating newly naturalized citizens (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/new-citizen-voting-honor-community/) after they cast their first ballot to watching young people become lifelong voters because someone took the time to explain the process (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/not-everyone-has-privilege-vote/), I know how important it is for every voter to have the power to decide the future of our country. That progress deserves careful protection, yet it stands in jeopardy this fall. Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), one of the many statewide ballot propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) California voters will tackle, essentially will make it harder for all voters to participate in future elections. If passed, it would require eligible voters to present a government-issued ID for in-person voting. It would also ask mail-in voters to provide the last four digits of a government ID on their ballots, which election officials would need to subsequently verify against their voter registration information. California’s voting law is already clear (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/frequently-asked-questions#voterreg): Any individual who wants to register to vote must state, under penalty of perjury, that they are a United States citizen. That requires everyone to provide information to verify their identity, such as a driver’s license or a social security number. Since California has a process in place to require all potential voters to prove their eligibility, Prop. 39 is a redundant step that will simply add new barriers for voters to cast a ballot. And it is already a federal crime (https://forumtogether.org/article/the-myths-and-truths-of-noncitizen-voting-in-the-united-states/) to vote if you are not a citizen. Should voters pass Prop. 39, millions of Californians could encounter difficulties at the ballot box and could be denied the right to participate in our elections — despite being eligible to vote. Chief among them would be the communities I have worked most closely with: Latinos and young people. Over 1 in 4 Latino adults (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) do not have a driver’s license that shows their current name or address, with 41% of youth, age 18-24, (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) in a similar predicament. As the political power of Latinos and young people grows with every election cycle, these measures are designed to undercut their influence in California policy and politics for generations to come. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/) Many eligible voters, particularly immigrant and mixed-status communities, already hesitate to engage with government systems out of concern for their privacy and how their personal information is used (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/04/california-dmv-shares-immigrant-driver-data/). Adding a new ID requirement may unintentionally deepen that hesitation, ultimately discouraging civic participation among eligible voters, while raising questions about implementation costs, data security and overall public trust. Proponents argue that presenting ID when voting deters fraud and maintains election integrity, but numerous studies have shown that voter fraud is astoundingly rare. According to the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice, voter fraud incidents have hovered between 0.0003% and 0.0025% (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth), making it virtually nonexistent. To add one final point, instituting more stringent voter identification processes would have major fiscal impacts to California taxpayers. As the state faces ongoing budget deficits, the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026) that creating a brand new form of identification — as Prop. 39 would mandate — could cost anywhere from tens of millions of dollars to the low hundreds of millions. Even if it is supposedly free to obtain, it carries a major price tag. Any reasonable Californian can agree that taxpayer funds should not be wasted on problems that do not exist. California is home to more than 27 million eligible voters (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/154day-primary-2026/complete-ror.pdf), making the state the largest individual democracy in the entire nation. In a moment when the nation is commemorating its 250th anniversary, now is not a time to make it more difficult to participate in our elections. Rather, Californians can live up to the ideals our founding fathers bequeathed to us all by ensuring every eligible Californian can participate confidently, freely and fully. Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) will help alleviate doubts in California’s vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/). Guest Commentary written by Bill Jones Bill Jones is a former California secretary of state. During two terms as California’s chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other. A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That’s why I’m supporting Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) on this November’s ballot. I hope Californians will join me. Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce. It doesn’t disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID (http://ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id) and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place. This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/voter-id-initiative-qualifies/) with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General’s office revised the official ballot title (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316615150.html) from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it “prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) California’s voter ID ballot measure would add unnecessary barriers to a secure system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/) That’s a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system. I’ve seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn’t vote twice. I can’t say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City’s mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote. California doesn’t quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting (https://calmatters.org/politics/2023/10/california-election-voting-republicans/) that simply didn’t exist when I ran elections as secretary of state. None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. Prop. 39 doesn’t solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California’s system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn’t partisan; it’s just good policy. Read more from CalMatters Text Get breaking news on your phone. How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

It would also ask mail-in voters to provide the last four digits of a government ID on their ballots, which election officials would need to subsequently verify against their voter registration information. California’s voting law is already clear (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/frequently-asked-questions#voterreg): Any individual who wants to register to vote must state, under penalty of perjury, that they are a United States citizen. That requires everyone to provide information to verify their identity, such as a driver’s license or a social security number. And it is already a federal crime (https://forumtogether.org/article/the-myths-and-truths-of-noncitizen-voting-in-the-united-states/) to vote if you are not a citizen. # Proposition 39
Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification.

## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California.
Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots.
The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
- ***In-Person Voting.*** When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
- ***Voting by Mail.*** When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope.

A **NO** vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

### Proposal
***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California.

I have a fair amount of solid information already, so next I want the strongest case for the "Yes" side. I'll read voteridca.org and the CalMatters pro commentary on voter ID. I also need the Berkeley IGS and PPIC October polls on Prop 39, then I'll check for any fact-checks.

Next I'm checking the figures being cited on each side. The "12 times more" Texas comparison looks roughly right, but the "over 100,000 signature rejections" claim seems too high next to the 2024 numbers, which put signature mismatches closer to 72,000. I'm also starting to think about whether legal challenges are likely, given how the measure would take effect upon passage.

Next I'm weighing whether a self-executing amendment would cause problems before the next election, since the first statewide contests may not come until the 2028 primary. I want the timeline and implementation details, so I'll look at the rest of the CBPC brief, especially the portion on how many Californians lack ID and what it would cost. I'll also check the LAO analysis page and Ballotpedia for legal challenges and the Yes campaign's claims.

I still want to check the post-election status, since the AP page showed no votes counted yet. I'll run a search for the Prop 39 results to see whether any outcome is already reported, even though I'm treating this as a question about voting ahead of time.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

Guest Commentary written by Marisol Ramirez Marisol Ramirez is a member of the Inland Empire Latino Giving Circle, advancing democratic participation, community leadership and equitable access to civic institutions. This November, Californians will head to the ballot box and participate in another election with real consequences for our communities. As a Latina and local philanthropist in the Inland Empire who has spent nearly two decades working to strengthen civic participation, I have learned that democracy is strongest when elections are both accessible and secure. From celebrating newly naturalized citizens (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/new-citizen-voting-honor-community/) after they cast their first ballot to watching young people become lifelong voters because someone took the time to explain the process (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/not-everyone-has-privilege-vote/), I know how important it is for every voter to have the power to decide the future of our country. That progress deserves careful protection, yet it stands in jeopardy this fall. Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), one of the many statewide ballot propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) California voters will tackle, essentially will make it harder for all voters to participate in future elections. If passed, it would require eligible voters to present a government-issued ID for in-person voting. It would also ask mail-in voters to provide the last four digits of a government ID on their ballots, which election officials would need to subsequently verify against their voter registration information. California’s voting law is already clear (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/frequently-asked-questions#voterreg): Any individual who wants to register to vote must state, under penalty of perjury, that they are a United States citizen. That requires everyone to provide information to verify their identity, such as a driver’s license or a social security number. Since California has a process in place to require all potential voters to prove their eligibility, Prop. 39 is a redundant step that will simply add new barriers for voters to cast a ballot. And it is already a federal crime (https://forumtogether.org/article/the-myths-and-truths-of-noncitizen-voting-in-the-united-states/) to vote if you are not a citizen. Should voters pass Prop. 39, millions of Californians could encounter difficulties at the ballot box and could be denied the right to participate in our elections — despite being eligible to vote. Chief among them would be the communities I have worked most closely with: Latinos and young people. Over 1 in 4 Latino adults (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) do not have a driver’s license that shows their current name or address, with 41% of youth, age 18-24, (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) in a similar predicament. As the political power of Latinos and young people grows with every election cycle, these measures are designed to undercut their influence in California policy and politics for generations to come. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/) Many eligible voters, particularly immigrant and mixed-status communities, already hesitate to engage with government systems out of concern for their privacy and how their personal information is used (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/04/california-dmv-shares-immigrant-driver-data/). Adding a new ID requirement may unintentionally deepen that hesitation, ultimately discouraging civic participation among eligible voters, while raising questions about implementation costs, data security and overall public trust. Proponents argue that presenting ID when voting deters fraud and maintains election integrity, but numerous studies have shown that voter fraud is astoundingly rare. According to the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice, voter fraud incidents have hovered between 0.0003% and 0.0025% (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth), making it virtually nonexistent. To add one final point, instituting more stringent voter identification processes would have major fiscal impacts to California taxpayers. As the state faces ongoing budget deficits, the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026) that creating a brand new form of identification — as Prop. 39 would mandate — could cost anywhere from tens of millions of dollars to the low hundreds of millions. Even if it is supposedly free to obtain, it carries a major price tag. Any reasonable Californian can agree that taxpayer funds should not be wasted on problems that do not exist. California is home to more than 27 million eligible voters (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/154day-primary-2026/complete-ror.pdf), making the state the largest individual democracy in the entire nation. In a moment when the nation is commemorating its 250th anniversary, now is not a time to make it more difficult to participate in our elections. Rather, Californians can live up to the ideals our founding fathers bequeathed to us all by ensuring every eligible Californian can participate confidently, freely and fully. California’s voter ID ballot measure would add unnecessary barriers to a secure system

By Marisol Ramirez, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a civic engagement advocate worries Proposition 39 will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system. The opposing view: A former state elections chief says the measure will help alleviate doubts in California's vote.

Guest Commentary written by

This November, Californians will head to the ballot box and participate in another election with real consequences for our communities.

As a Latina and local philanthropist in the Inland Empire who has spent nearly two decades working to strengthen civic participation, I have learned that democracy is strongest when elections are both accessible and secure. 

From celebrating newly naturalized citizens after they cast their first ballot to watching young people become lifelong voters because someone took the time to explain the process, I know how important it is for every voter to have the power to decide the future of our country.

That progress deserves careful protection, yet it stands in jeopardy this fall.

## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California.
Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots.
The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
- ***In-Person Voting.*** When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.

Proposition 4
The basics
Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on the public funding of campaigns and allow all local and state governments to offer public financing programs with certain conditions.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 4: Allowing public campaign financing in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)
Prop 4 would repeal California’s 1988 ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to create programs for candidates seeking office.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Candidates would have to abide by certain expenditure limits and follow strict criteria. Funds could not be used for legal or defense purposes or to repay personal loans, nor could they be pulled from education, transportation or public safety buckets. The ballot measure also prohibits discrimination based on party or whether a candidate is an incumbent or running in opposition.
Dig deeper
Democrats and many good government groups support it. The California Taxpayers Assn. and Reform California oppose it.
Proposition 5
The basics
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Advertisement
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide)
Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Dig deeper
California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the Progressive era (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.
But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.
After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.

Proposition 37
The basics
California’s Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained) would authorize up to $25 billion in down-payment loans for eligible middle-income buyers.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Prop. 37 offers $25 billion to homebuyers to help with a down payment. Here’s the catch (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained)
California’s Prop. 37 could provide $25 billion for homebuyer down payments. Learn how the middle-class housing measure works and its key caveats.
Oct. 24, 2026
The impact
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds. The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building. The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.
Dig deeper
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José. Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction. But critics warn down-payment debt could burden buyers and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.
Proposition 38
The basics
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year. Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 38: Immunology and immunotherapy research funding (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide)
Prop 38 aims to fund immunotherapy research to prevent and cure diseases through bonds. An opponent says it is a debt-financed model that prioritizes a few diseases.
Oct. 26, 2026
The impact
The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s. It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The Yes on 38 campaign says the proposition pays for itself; 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the state to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. However, it’s difficult to predict whether any research projects will lead to marketable treatments.
Dig deeper
Proposition 38 was backed by organizations including the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research and the ALS Assn. as well as a majority of local chapters of Democratic organizations across the state. Supporters say the proposed funding could give those afflicted with chronic illness hope and potentially more options for treatment.
Its opponents have said the proposed criteria for awarding the grant funding would appear to create an extremely small pool of qualified recipients. Only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, co-founded by billionaire Gary K. Michelson, would qualify under the proposed criteria, according to No on 38.
Advertisement
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for Yes on 38, said “lots of institutions would qualify for funds under this measure.” But she said at a virtual news conference in mid-September that it was “very likely” that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy “will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria.”
Ultimately, Swanson said, the decision lies with the California Department of Public Health.

Proposition 39
The basics
Proposition 39 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-39-voting-id-requirements-voter-guide) would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote. In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected.

The impact
Opponents contend — as do many independent election experts — that California already has robust measures for verifying the eligibility and identity of voters, and that voter fraud, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare. The measure is opposed by the state’s Democratic establishment and prominent civil rights groups, who say it will disenfranchise many eligible voters, particularly those of color, who are poor or live in rural communities. Backers — who include prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump — say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. They have provided little evidence of widespread fraud.

Proposition 41
The basics
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Proposition 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)

Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Dig deeper
The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41. In arguments against the measure, SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote that the billionaires don’t care about government accountability and have been avoiding higher taxes through loopholes and tax breaks.

The basics
Proposition 42 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide) would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.

Proposition 5
The basics
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Advertisement
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide)
Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Dig deeper
California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the Progressive era (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.
But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.
After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.

I'm not going to give a bare yes or no. Prop 39 is a contested political question, and the right vote depends on how you weigh ballot access, added verification, cost, and trust in elections. That's your judgment to make. Here is what the research shows.

**What it does** (Yes adopts it; No keeps today's signature-based verification)
- **ID requirement:** In person, you show government ID. By mail, you write the last four digits of a pre-designated ID number on the envelope, and it must match your registration. The state issues a free voter ID card on request.
- **Citizenship checks:** Officials must use "best efforts" and "government data" to verify voters' citizenship and report the results by county. The State Auditor reviews compliance every odd-numbered year, and citizens can sue over compliance.
- **Details left open:** It's a constitutional amendment, so the Legislature would define key details, such as which IDs count and what "best efforts" means. The text doesn't say whether or how a mismatched ballot could be corrected.
- **Cost:** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

**What the evidence shows**
- **Fraud:** Reviews by the Brennan Center and the Cato Institute find documented in-person impersonation and noncitizen voting too rare to affect outcomes. Supporters say the aim is deterrence and public confidence.
- **Turnout and rejections:** Studies of polling-place ID laws mostly find small turnout effects, and a prominent 2021 study found none. Mail ballots are less settled. In its first statewide election under a similar ID-number rule, Texas rejected 12.4% of mail ballots (March 2022 primary), versus 0.8% in 2020. Prop 39 differs in some ways, such as requiring the chosen ID type to be noted on the envelope, so California's results would depend on implementation. California rejected about 0.9% of mail ballots in 2024, roughly 71,000 of them for signature mismatches, which supporters cite as a flaw in the current system.
- **Citizenship data:** No comprehensive citizenship database exists. ProPublica and the Texas Tribune found that the federal SAVE tool has wrongly flagged some naturalized citizens. The measure doesn't say what data would be used.

**Who's where**
- **Yes:** The California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the OC Register editorial board, and former Secretary of State Bill Jones. Their case is that ID is routine (36 states ask for it), the card is free, and signature matching is a flawed check.
- **No:** The California Democratic Party, ACLU, Common Cause, the League of Women Voters, and the Sacramento Bee, SF Chronicle, Mercury News and San Diego Union-Tribune editorial boards. Their case is that it targets a rare problem, risks rejecting valid ballots, and adds cost and privacy risk. The Union-Tribune said the ID rule itself isn't clearly onerous but objected to the citizenship mandate.

The arguments in the official guide aren't fact-checked, and proponents challenged the ballot title as misleading (a judge upheld it). If you tell me what matters most to you, I can show how Prop 39 lines up with it. I can also make the strongest case for either side.

In this world, however, the stakes seem to be considerably lower.
That’s the conclusion of a new study, one of the largest to date, from the economists Enrico Cantoni and Vincent Pons, which assessed the impact of voter ID laws between 2008 and 2016 using a nationwide voter file.
The study finds that requiring voter identification has no effect on turnout — not overall, and not on “any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.”
If that shocks you, it shouldn’t.
The evidence that voter ID laws meaningfully suppress minority votes has always been shaky; a literature review in 2017 that filtered out studies with obvious design flaws reported “modest, if any, turnout effects of voter identification laws” in the best research on the subject.
So a voter ID requirement might possibly affect the closest of close races, based on what we’ve learned up till now — but if the Cantoni and Pons results hold up, the real effect is basically nil.

I have a fair amount of solid information already, so next I want the strongest case for the "Yes" side. I'll read voteridca.org and the CalMatters pro commentary on voter ID. I also need the Berkeley IGS and PPIC October polls on Prop 39, then I'll check for any fact-checks.

Next I'm checking the figures being cited on each side. The "12 times more" Texas comparison looks roughly right, but the "over 100,000 signature rejections" claim seems too high next to the 2024 numbers, which put signature mismatches closer to 72,000. I'm also starting to think about whether legal challenges are likely, given how the measure would take effect upon passage.

Next I'm weighing whether a self-executing amendment would cause problems before the next election, since the first statewide contests may not come until the 2028 primary. I want the timeline and implementation details, so I'll look at the rest of the CBPC brief, especially the portion on how many Californians lack ID and what it would cost. I'll also check the LAO analysis page and Ballotpedia for legal challenges and the Yes campaign's claims.

I still want to check the post-election status, since the AP page showed no votes counted yet. I'll run a search for the Prop 39 results to see whether any outcome is already reported, even though I'm treating this as a question about voting ahead of time.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

Guest Commentary written by Marisol Ramirez Marisol Ramirez is a member of the Inland Empire Latino Giving Circle, advancing democratic participation, community leadership and equitable access to civic institutions. This November, Californians will head to the ballot box and participate in another election with real consequences for our communities. As a Latina and local philanthropist in the Inland Empire who has spent nearly two decades working to strengthen civic participation, I have learned that democracy is strongest when elections are both accessible and secure. From celebrating newly naturalized citizens (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/new-citizen-voting-honor-community/) after they cast their first ballot to watching young people become lifelong voters because someone took the time to explain the process (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/not-everyone-has-privilege-vote/), I know how important it is for every voter to have the power to decide the future of our country. That progress deserves careful protection, yet it stands in jeopardy this fall. Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), one of the many statewide ballot propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) California voters will tackle, essentially will make it harder for all voters to participate in future elections. If passed, it would require eligible voters to present a government-issued ID for in-person voting. It would also ask mail-in voters to provide the last four digits of a government ID on their ballots, which election officials would need to subsequently verify against their voter registration information. California’s voting law is already clear (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/frequently-asked-questions#voterreg): Any individual who wants to register to vote must state, under penalty of perjury, that they are a United States citizen. That requires everyone to provide information to verify their identity, such as a driver’s license or a social security number. Since California has a process in place to require all potential voters to prove their eligibility, Prop. 39 is a redundant step that will simply add new barriers for voters to cast a ballot. And it is already a federal crime (https://forumtogether.org/article/the-myths-and-truths-of-noncitizen-voting-in-the-united-states/) to vote if you are not a citizen. Should voters pass Prop. 39, millions of Californians could encounter difficulties at the ballot box and could be denied the right to participate in our elections — despite being eligible to vote. Chief among them would be the communities I have worked most closely with: Latinos and young people. Over 1 in 4 Latino adults (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) do not have a driver’s license that shows their current name or address, with 41% of youth, age 18-24, (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) in a similar predicament. As the political power of Latinos and young people grows with every election cycle, these measures are designed to undercut their influence in California policy and politics for generations to come. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/) Many eligible voters, particularly immigrant and mixed-status communities, already hesitate to engage with government systems out of concern for their privacy and how their personal information is used (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/04/california-dmv-shares-immigrant-driver-data/). Adding a new ID requirement may unintentionally deepen that hesitation, ultimately discouraging civic participation among eligible voters, while raising questions about implementation costs, data security and overall public trust. Proponents argue that presenting ID when voting deters fraud and maintains election integrity, but numerous studies have shown that voter fraud is astoundingly rare. According to the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice, voter fraud incidents have hovered between 0.0003% and 0.0025% (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth), making it virtually nonexistent. To add one final point, instituting more stringent voter identification processes would have major fiscal impacts to California taxpayers. As the state faces ongoing budget deficits, the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026) that creating a brand new form of identification — as Prop. 39 would mandate — could cost anywhere from tens of millions of dollars to the low hundreds of millions. Even if it is supposedly free to obtain, it carries a major price tag. Any reasonable Californian can agree that taxpayer funds should not be wasted on problems that do not exist. California is home to more than 27 million eligible voters (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/154day-primary-2026/complete-ror.pdf), making the state the largest individual democracy in the entire nation. In a moment when the nation is commemorating its 250th anniversary, now is not a time to make it more difficult to participate in our elections. Rather, Californians can live up to the ideals our founding fathers bequeathed to us all by ensuring every eligible Californian can participate confidently, freely and fully. Proposition 4
The basics
Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on the public funding of campaigns and allow all local and state governments to offer public financing programs with certain conditions.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 4: Allowing public campaign financing in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)
Prop 4 would repeal California’s 1988 ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to create programs for candidates seeking office.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Candidates would have to abide by certain expenditure limits and follow strict criteria. Funds could not be used for legal or defense purposes or to repay personal loans, nor could they be pulled from education, transportation or public safety buckets. The ballot measure also prohibits discrimination based on party or whether a candidate is an incumbent or running in opposition.
Dig deeper
Democrats and many good government groups support it. The California Taxpayers Assn. and Reform California oppose it.
Proposition 5
The basics
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Advertisement
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide)
Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Dig deeper
California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the Progressive era (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.
But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.
After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.

Proposition 37
The basics
California’s Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained) would authorize up to $25 billion in down-payment loans for eligible middle-income buyers.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Prop. 37 offers $25 billion to homebuyers to help with a down payment. Here’s the catch (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained)
California’s Prop. 37 could provide $25 billion for homebuyer down payments. Learn how the middle-class housing measure works and its key caveats.
Oct. 24, 2026
The impact
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds. The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building. The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.
Dig deeper
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José. Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction. But critics warn down-payment debt could burden buyers and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.
Proposition 38
The basics
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year. Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.

Your guide to Proposition 38: Immunology and immunotherapy research funding (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide)
Prop 38 aims to fund immunotherapy research to prevent and cure diseases through bonds. An opponent says it is a debt-financed model that prioritizes a few diseases.
Oct. 26, 2026
The impact
The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s. It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The Yes on 38 campaign says the proposition pays for itself; 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the state to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. However, it’s difficult to predict whether any research projects will lead to marketable treatments.

Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some of California’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they have spent a fortune in an effort to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.
Advertisement
More reading
A powerful union and the birth of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) (L.A. Times)
Why unions are divided over Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-30/labor-organizers-spearheading-california-billionaire-tax-rebuffed-by-parent-union) (L.A. Times)
The Google co-founder fighting the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax) (L.A. Times)
Inside the massive spending to defeat Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) (L.A. Times)
How the billionaire tax could spark national movement (https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/10/12/the-battle-to-pass-a-billionaire-tax) (The New Yorker)
The academics behind Prop. 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) (Sacramento Bee)
Will Prop. 40 really bring an exodus? (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus) (L.A. Times)
Why healthcare is divided by Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/science/story/2026-09-28/billionaire-tax-is-dividing-california-healthcare-system-its-designed-to-support) (Bloomberg)
Taxing the “ultrarich,” a guide (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/13/magazine/billionaire-wealth-tax-proposition-40.html) (New York Times)
Proposition 41
The basics
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Proposition 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Dig deeper
The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41. In arguments against the measure, SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote that the billionaires don’t care about government accountability and have been avoiding higher taxes through loopholes and tax breaks.
Proposition 42
The basics
Proposition 42 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide) would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
Advertisement
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.
“Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California — we need protection against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings,” supporters wrote in favor of the measure. The California Small Business Assn., California Senior Alliance, California Professional Firefighters and other groups back the measure.
“Don’t be fooled — Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes,” SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote in arguments against the proposition. “It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes.”
Proposition 44
The basics
Proposition 44 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-44-health-clinic-spending-voter-guide) asks voters to require federally funded community health centers to spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on “program services advancing their charitable purpose.”

California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 44: Federally funded health clinic spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-44-health-clinic-spending-voter-guide)
Prop 44 asks voters to require federally funded community health centers to spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on “program services advancing their charitable purpose.”
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
If the proposition passes, the state attorney general will be responsible for determining what services fall into that category

I'm not going to give a bare yes or no. Prop 39 is a contested political question, and the right vote depends on how you weigh ballot access, added verification, cost, and trust in elections. That's your judgment to make. Here is what the research shows.

**What it does** (Yes adopts it; No keeps today's signature-based verification)
- **ID requirement:** In person, you show government ID. By mail, you write the last four digits of a pre-designated ID number on the envelope, and it must match your registration. The state issues a free voter ID card on request.
- **Citizenship checks:** Officials must use "best efforts" and "government data" to verify voters' citizenship and report the results by county. The State Auditor reviews compliance every odd-numbered year, and citizens can sue over compliance.
- **Details left open:** It's a constitutional amendment, so the Legislature would define key details, such as which IDs count and what "best efforts" means. The text doesn't say whether or how a mismatched ballot could be corrected.
- **Cost:** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

**What the evidence shows**
- **Fraud:** Reviews by the Brennan Center and the Cato Institute find documented in-person impersonation and noncitizen voting too rare to affect outcomes. Supporters say the aim is deterrence and public confidence.
- **Turnout and rejections:** Studies of polling-place ID laws mostly find small turnout effects, and a prominent 2021 study found none. Mail ballots are less settled. In its first statewide election under a similar ID-number rule, Texas rejected 12.4% of mail ballots (March 2022 primary), versus 0.8% in 2020. Prop 39 differs in some ways, such as requiring the chosen ID type to be noted on the envelope, so California's results would depend on implementation. California rejected about 0.9% of mail ballots in 2024, roughly 71,000 of them for signature mismatches, which supporters cite as a flaw in the current system.
- **Citizenship data:** No comprehensive citizenship database exists. ProPublica and the Texas Tribune found that the federal SAVE tool has wrongly flagged some naturalized citizens. The measure doesn't say what data would be used.

**Who's where**
- **Yes:** The California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the OC Register editorial board, and former Secretary of State Bill Jones. Their case is that ID is routine (36 states ask for it), the card is free, and signature matching is a flawed check.
- **No:** The California Democratic Party, ACLU, Common Cause, the League of Women Voters, and the Sacramento Bee, SF Chronicle, Mercury News and San Diego Union-Tribune editorial boards. Their case is that it targets a rare problem, risks rejecting valid ballots, and adds cost and privacy risk. The Union-Tribune said the ID rule itself isn't clearly onerous but objected to the citizenship mandate.

The arguments in the official guide aren't fact-checked, and proponents challenged the ballot title as misleading (a judge upheld it). If you tell me what matters most to you, I can show how Prop 39 lines up with it. I can also make the strongest case for either side.
